summary.text: Direct finite minimality checks handle the powers \(9\) and \(27\); for \(81\), expanding place values via \(10^i\equiv1+9i\pmod{81}\) for a number and its reversal forces any smaller candidate’s digit sum to be \(81\), hence all nine digits to be \(9\). For larger powers, the palindrome \(68899199886\) and then repetitions of its 11-digit block give strictly smaller witnesses, with the associated geometric-series factor supplying each additional power of \(3\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(x)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(x\); any zeros that become leading zeros after reversal are, as usual, discarded. For a positive integer \(m\), the definition of \(a(m)\) is equivalently
\[
a(m)=\min\{x>0:m\mid x\text{ and }m\mid R(x)\},
\]
provided this set is nonempty. Indeed, writing \(x=km\), this is the same as choosing the least positive multiplier \(k\) for which \(m\mid R(km)\). Consequently, to prove an upper bound for \(a(m)\), it suffices to exhibit one positive admissible \(x\), and to prove an exact value it suffices additionally to rule out every smaller positive multiple of \(m\).

We prove that, for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

First we establish the three cases in which equality holds.

For \(n=2\), the number \(9\) is divisible by \(9\), and its reversal is itself. There is no smaller positive multiple of \(9\). Thus
\[
a(9)=9=10^{3^0}-1.
\]

For \(n=3\), \(999=37\cdot27\), and \(R(999)=999\), so \(999\) is admissible for \(27\). To see that it is the least admissible number, it is enough to examine the positive multiples \(27j\) for \(1\le j\le36\). The following table gives \(27j\), its reversal, and in parentheses the residue of that reversal modulo \(27\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c@{\qquad}c|c|c}
j&27j&R(27j)\bmod27&j&27j&R(27j)\bmod27\\ \hline
1&27&72\ (18)&19&513&315\ (18)\\
2&54&45\ (18)&20&540&45\ (18)\\
3&81&18\ (18)&21&567&765\ (9)\\
4&108&801\ (18)&22&594&495\ (9)\\
5&135&531\ (18)&23&621&126\ (18)\\
6&162&261\ (18)&24&648&846\ (9)\\
7&189&981\ (9)&25&675&576\ (9)\\
8&216&612\ (18)&26&702&207\ (18)\\
9&243&342\ (18)&27&729&927\ (9)\\
10&270&72\ (18)&28&756&657\ (9)\\
11&297&792\ (9)&29&783&387\ (9)\\
12&324&423\ (18)&30&810&18\ (18)\\
13&351&153\ (18)&31&837&738\ (9)\\
14&378&873\ (9)&32&864&468\ (9)\\
15&405&504\ (18)&33&891&198\ (9)\\
16&432&234\ (18)&34&918&819\ (9)\\
17&459&954\ (9)&35&945&549\ (9)\\
18&486&684\ (9)&36&972&279\ (9)
\end{array}
\]
None of these residues is zero. Hence no positive multiple of \(27\) below \(999\) has reversal divisible by \(27\), and therefore
\[
a(27)=999=10^{3^1}-1.
\]

The case \(n=4\), that is, modulus \(81\), requires a more general digit argument. We will show that no positive integer less than \(999999999\) can have both itself and its reversal divisible by \(81\).

Write the decimal digits of a positive integer \(x<10^9\), starting with the units digit, as
\[
L=(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell-1}),
\qquad
x=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i10^i.
\]
Here \(1\le\ell\le9\), every \(d_i\) lies between \(0\) and \(9\), and the most significant digit \(d_{\ell-1}\) is nonzero. Put
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i,
\qquad
T=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}i d_i.
\]
Because \(10=1+9\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv1+9i\pmod{81}.
\]
Thus
\[
x\equiv S+9T\pmod{81}.
\]
For the reversed digit list, the digit \(d_i\) has weight \(\ell-1-i\). If
\[
T_R=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(\ell-1-i)d_i,
\]
then similarly
\[
R(x)\equiv S+9T_R\pmod{81}.
\]
(The same formula remains correct when the original number ends in zero, since the reversed expression simply has a leading zero.) Moreover,
\[
T+T_R=\sum_i\bigl(i+(\ell-1-i)\bigr)d_i=(\ell-1)S.
\]

Suppose now that \(81\mid x\) and \(81\mid R(x)\). The two preceding congruences yield
\[
S+9T\equiv0\pmod{81},
\qquad
S+9T_R\equiv0\pmod{81}.
\]
Adding them and using \(T+T_R=(\ell-1)S\), we obtain
\[
\bigl(2+9(\ell-1)\bigr)S\equiv0\pmod{81}.
\]
The coefficient \(2+9(\ell-1)\) is congruent to \(2\) modulo \(3\), and hence is relatively prime to \(81=3^4\). It can therefore be cancelled modulo \(81\), giving
\[
81\mid S.
\]

On the other hand, because there are at most nine digits and each is at most \(9\),
\[
0<S\le9\ell\le81.
\]
The strict positivity follows from the nonzero most significant digit. Thus \(S=81\). Equality in the bounds above forces \(\ell=9\), and then nine digits each at most \(9\) can have sum \(81\) only if every digit equals \(9\). Therefore \(x=999999999\).

We have proved that there is no positive \(x<999999999\) for which both \(x\) and \(R(x)\) are divisible by \(81\). The number \(999999999\) itself is admissible: it is a palindrome, and
\[
999999999=81\cdot12345679.
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(81)=999999999=10^{3^2}-1.
\]
This completes the proof of the equality for \(n=2,3,4\).

It remains to prove that equality fails for every \(n\ge5\). We do this by constructing admissible palindromes strictly smaller than the proposed all-nines number.

Consider the eleven-digit palindrome
\[
B=68899199886.
\]
Its factorization includes a large power of \(3\):
\[
B=3^{12}\cdot129646
  =2\cdot3^{12}\cdot11\cdot71\cdot83.
\]
Thus \(3^n\mid B\) for every \(5\le n\le12\). Since \(R(B)=B\), the number \(B\) is admissible for every modulus \(3^n\) in this range, so
\[
a(3^n)\le B\qquad(5\le n\le12).
\]
For these exponents, \(3^{n-2}\ge3^3=27>11\), while
\[
B=68899199886<10^{11}-1.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(3^n)\le B<10^{11}-1<10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\qquad(5\le n\le12).
\]
In particular, the desired equality fails throughout this finite range.

For all larger \(n\), we use repetitions of the same palindromic block. Set
\[
q=10^{11}
\]
and, for \(t\ge1\), define
\[
G_t=1+q+q^2+\cdots+q^{t-1},
\qquad
P_t=B G_t.
\]
In decimal notation, \(P_t\) is obtained by writing the block \(68899199886\) exactly \(t\) times consecutively. Since the block itself is a palindrome and all the repeated blocks are identical, the entire \(11t\)-digit string is a palindrome. Hence
\[
R(P_t)=P_t.
\]
All digits of the block are nonzero, so there is no issue with a dropped leading or trailing zero. Also,
\[
0<P_t<10^{11t},
\]
since it has exactly \(11t\) decimal digits.

We next establish the divisibility property
\[
3^r\mid G_{3^r}\qquad(r\ge0).
\]
This follows by induction on \(r\). For \(r=0\), \(G_{3^0}=G_1=1\), which is divisible by \(3^0=1\). For the induction step, the geometric sum satisfies, for every positive \(m\),
\[
G_{3m}=G_m\bigl(1+q^m+q^{2m}\bigr).
\]
Since \(q=10^{11}\equiv1\pmod3\),
\[
1+q^m+q^{2m}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
If \(3^r\mid G_{3^r}\), taking \(m=3^r\) in the displayed factorization shows that
\[
3^{r+1}\mid G_{3^{r+1}}.
\]
This proves the claim for all \(r\).

Now let \(n\ge13\), put
\[
r=n-12,
\qquad
t=3^r=3^{n-12}.
\]
Because \(3^{12}\mid B\) and \(3^r\mid G_{3^r}=G_t\), we have
\[
3^n=3^{12+r}\mid B G_t=P_t.
\]
The number \(P_t\) is positive and is its own reversal, so it is admissible for \(3^n\). Therefore
\[
a(3^n)\le P_t.
\]
It remains only to compare its size with the proposed value. We have
\[
P_t<10^{11t}.
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
3^{n-2}=3^{(n-12)+10}=3^{n-12}\,3^{10}=59049t.
\]
Since \(11t<59049t\),
\[
10^{11t}<10^{3^{n-2}}.
\]
Both sides are integers, and in fact the intermediate powers of ten are separated by far more than one; explicitly,
\[
P_t<10^{11t}\le 10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Thus
\[
a(3^n)\le P_t<10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\qquad(n\ge13).
\]
So equality also fails for every \(n\ge13\).

Combining the two ranges, for every \(n\ge5\) we have the strict inequality
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Finally, if \(n\ge2\), then either \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\), in which case the three exact computations above prove equality, or else \(n\ge5\), in which case the strict upper bound proves inequality. Hence
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\text{if and only if}\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\},
\]
as required.
